why.Isaiah 52:13-53:12: The whole servant song. Read it as one unit. This case is about how Jewish sources read these fifteen verses, not about any single line.
why.Isaiah 53:4-5: The two verses the Jewish sources pick up. Sanhedrin 98b quotes 'borne our griefs' from 53:4. Ruth Rabbah applies 53:5 to the Messiah.
why.Acts 8:32-35: An Ethiopian official reads Isaiah 53 and asks who it is about. The oldest Christian answer, and it starts as a question.
why.Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 52:13: The old Aramaic version read aloud in synagogues. It opens the passage 'Behold, my servant the Messiah.' Strong for you, and Jewish in origin.
why.Sanhedrin 98b: A page of the Talmud asking what the Messiah's name is. One answer points to Isaiah 53:4. Jewish, and not written to help Christians.
why.Ruth Rabbah 5:6: An early Jewish sermon collection on the book of Ruth. It applies Isaiah 53:5, the wounding, to the Messiah's own suffering.
why.Alshich on Isaiah 52:13: Moshe Alshich, a Jewish commentator in Safed in the 1500s. He wrote that 'our rabbis with one voice' read the passage of King Messiah.
why.Yom Kippur Musaf piyyut 'Az milifnei ber: An old poem in Ashkenazi prayer books for the Day of Atonement. It speaks of 'our righteous anointed' who carries our sins.

why.Isaiah 52:13-53:12: The passage both sides read. The argument here is made from inside it, not from other chapters. Read the whole song first.
why.Isaiah 49:5-6: An earlier servant song. Here the servant has a mission to Israel: to bring Jacob back. A servant sent to a people is not that people.
why.Isaiah 42:24-25: Isaiah says Israel was plundered because Israel sinned. That is his normal verdict on the nation. It sits badly beside the innocent servant of 53:9.
why.Jeremiah 31:35-37: God ties Israel's survival to the sun and moon: the nation never ceases. The servant dies. That is the sharpest point in this case.
why.Luke 22:37: Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 of himself, hours before his arrest. A Christian source, so it settles nothing on its own.
why.1 Peter 2:22-25: Quotes 53:9 of Jesus: 'no deceit in his mouth.' That innocence clause is the one Israel's own prophets never grant the nation.
why.Rashi on Isaiah 53: Rashi, the French rabbi whose commentary became standard after about 1100. He reads the servant as Israel. Strong for the Jewish side.
why.Ibn Ezra on Isaiah 53: A Spanish commentator of the 1100s who also reads the servant as Israel. Cite him to show Rashi was not alone in this.
why.Origen, Contra Celsum 1.55 (attesting th: A Christian writer around 248 AD reports Jews already reading the servant as Israel. Proof that reading is ancient, not a medieval invention.

why.Zechariah 12:10-12: The mourning passage. Sukkah 52a hangs the death of Messiah son of Joseph on it. Both traditions are reading the same verse.
why.Isaiah 53:12: The servant 'poured out his soul unto death.' This is the dying picture the two-Messiah scheme was built to account for.
why.Isaiah 9:6-7: The other picture: a child born, the government on his shoulder, ruling on David's throne. The reigning king half of the problem.
why.Zechariah 9:9: The king enters Jerusalem 'lowly, and riding upon an ass.' A humble arrival, not a conquest. Part of why the pictures resist merging.
why.Luke 24:25-27: On the Emmaus road Jesus says the Messiah had to suffer first and enter glory after. The Christian answer in one sentence.
why.Hebrews 9:28: Says Christ will 'appear the second time.' The two-comings answer rests here, and the Jewish reply calls it a patch that cannot be tested.
why.John 19:37: Applies Zechariah 12:10 to the crucifixion. Sukkah 52a applies the same verse to a slain Messiah. That overlap is the case.
why.Sukkah 52a: The Talmud page naming two Messiahs: son of Joseph, who is killed, and son of David, who reigns. Judaism's own answer to the two pictures.
why.Pesikta Rabbati 36-37: A collection of Jewish sermons for feast days. It describes a Messiah who accepts terrible suffering for Israel. Not Christian, and not fringe.

why.Daniel 9:24-27: The seventy weeks passage. The date maths here is genuinely argued about. The order of events is not, and the order is what this case uses.
why.Daniel 9:26: The verse the case rests on. An anointed one is 'cut off,' then the city and sanctuary are destroyed. Cut off first. Temple second.
why.Luke 19:41-44: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and foretells the siege, saying she missed 'the time of thy visitation.' A Christian text, so it proves nothing alone.
why.Mark 1:15: 'The time is fulfilled.' Jesus opens his preaching with a claim about the clock, which is why Daniel's timetable matters to Christians.
why.Seder Olam Rabbah 28-30: The classic Jewish chronology, from about 200 AD. It runs Daniel's 490 years down to the Temple's fall. Jewish arithmetic, ending in 70 AD.
why.Rashi on Daniel 9:26: Rashi reads the cut-off anointed one as King Agrippa, at the fall of the Temple. Against you on who. With you on when.
why.Sanhedrin 97b: The Talmud curses those who calculate when the end will come. Strong for the Jewish side, and a fair warning against date maths.

why.Micah 5:2 (5:1 Heb): The verse itself. Note the two numbering systems: Hebrew Bibles print it as 5:1. Expect your friend to open a different verse number.
why.Isaiah 9:6-7: The child called 'mighty God' on David's throne. Christians read it beside Micah's 'from everlasting.' Suggestive, but the Hebrew does not force it.
why.Matthew 2:1-6: Herod asks where the Messiah is to be born and the chief priests answer with Micah. The Gospel records it as the standard Jewish answer.
why.Luke 2:1-7: The other birth account, with the census. It is also where the history gets hard: Quirinius governed about a decade after Herod died.
why.John 7:41-42: A crowd argues the Messiah comes from Bethlehem, not Galilee. The point is small but useful. The hope was ordinary, not made up later.
why.Targum Jonathan on Micah 5:1: The old Aramaic synagogue version. It reads 'from you shall come forth before Me the Messiah.' A Jewish source granting the messianic reading.
why.Rashi on Micah 5:1: Rashi glosses it 'from you shall emerge for Me Messiah son of David.' The leading medieval Jewish commentator, granting the same point.
why.Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4 (Messiah a: A Talmud story where the Messiah is born in Bethlehem on the day the Temple falls. Legend, not proof, but the pairing was already Jewish.

why.Zechariah 12:10-14: The passage itself. Watch the switch inside one sentence: look on 'me,' mourn for 'him.' That oddity is in the Hebrew, not the English.
why.Zechariah 13:1: The very next verse opens a fountain 'for sin and for uncleanness.' Piercing, then mourning, then cleansing, in that order.
why.Zechariah 13:7: 'Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.' A second struck figure a few lines later, which Matthew 26:31 picks up.
why.John 19:34-37: Quotes Zechariah 12:10 at the spear thrust. This is the Christian application, so it carries no weight with a Jewish reader by itself.
why.Revelation 1:7: Uses the same verse of the return rather than the cross. Worth knowing, because it shows the New Testament puts the mourning still ahead.
why.Matthew 26:31: Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7 the night he is arrested. Shows the Gospel writers were reading this whole section, not one stray verse.
why.Sukkah 52a: The Talmud applies this mourning to Messiah son of Joseph, who is killed. A Jewish source arriving at a pierced, slain Messiah on its own.
why.Rashi on Zechariah 12:10: Rashi cites the slain-Messiah tradition, but as a warrior killed at the end of history. He grants the figure and denies the atoning death.

why.Psalm 22:1-31: The whole psalm. Read it start to finish. The parts that need no argument outnumber the one disputed word by a long way.
why.Psalm 22:16(17): The contested verse, numbered 17 in Hebrew Bibles. This is the 'like a lion' or 'they pierced' problem, and it is genuinely unsettled.
why.Psalm 22:18: 'They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.' Nobody disputes this verse. It is the one to read aloud.
why.Matthew 27:35-46: Jesus quotes verse 1 from the cross, and soldiers divide his clothes. A Christian source, so give away verse 16 before you lean on it.
why.John 19:23-24: Names Psalm 22:18 directly at the dividing of the clothes. The clearest New Testament use of this psalm, and it is not verse 16.
why.Rashi on Psalm 22: Rashi reads the psalm as David's own lament, and takes verse 16 as 'like a lion.' The standard Jewish reading, and a reasonable one.
why.Midrash Tehillim 22 (applied to Esther): An old Jewish commentary on Psalms that reads this psalm of Esther. Good evidence that Jewish tradition never fixed it on the Messiah.

why.Genesis 49:10: The verse. Jacob keeps the ruler's staff with Judah 'until Shiloh come.' Everything here hangs on one unclear word and one disputed date.
why.Matthew 1:1-3: Traces Jesus to Judah through Perez. It matters only because the verse is about Judah's line, and this is the claim that he stands in it.
why.Revelation 5:5: Calls Jesus 'the Lion of the tribe of Juda,' picking up Jacob's lion image one verse earlier. Christian use, not evidence.
why.Targum Onkelos on Genesis 49:10: The Aramaic Torah version used in synagogues. It renders Shiloh as 'the Messiah, whose is the kingdom.' A Jewish source making the identification.
why.Sanhedrin 98b: The Talmud page listing names for the Messiah. 'Shiloh' is one of them. Jewish, and long before any argument with Christians.
why.Rashi on Genesis 49:10: Rashi glosses Shiloh as 'the King Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs.' The identification is common ground. The timing is not.
why.Avodah Zarah 8b: The Talmud says the courts lost power over capital cases forty years before the Temple fell. Christians build a clock on it. Handle with care.

why.Isaiah 7:14-16: Read all three verses, not just the first. Verse 16 ties the child's early years to two kings falling in Ahaz's own lifetime.
why.Isaiah 8:8-10: Immanuel is named again here, inside the same crisis. Evidence that the child belongs to Isaiah's own century.
why.Isaiah 9:6-7: The divine child of the next chapter. Any Christian case for reading Immanuel forward rests here, not on the word almah.
why.Genesis 24:43: Rebekah is called an almah at the well. Shows the word means a young woman of marrying age. This one cuts against the Christian reading.
why.Matthew 1:22-23: Matthew quotes the Greek version's 'virgin.' This is Matthew explaining a birth he already believed, not the reason he believed it.
why.Matthew 2:15: Matthew calls Hosea 11:1 'fulfilled' by Jesus, though Hosea was writing about Israel. Proof that 'fulfil' here means filling out a pattern.
why.Luke 1:34-35: Luke's account of the virgin birth never mentions Isaiah 7:14. Useful: the doctrine does not stand or fall with this verse.
why.Rashi on Isaiah 7:14: Rashi reads the sign as a child born in Ahaz's own day. Strong for the Jewish side, and the chapter supports him.
why.Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 67 (: A Christian record of a Jew making this exact objection around 160 AD. The objection is not modern, and it was never answered well.

why.Isaiah 61:1-2: 'Good tidings unto the meek.' The Isaiah text underneath both the scroll and Jesus's answer to John. Read it to see what was expected.
why.Isaiah 35:5-6: Blind eyes opened, lame men leaping. The other Isaiah passage behind that list. Note what is missing from both: raising the dead.
why.Luke 7:18-23: John the Baptist asks 'art thou he?' Jesus answers with the scroll's own list, dead raised included. That extra item is the point.
why.Matthew 11:2-6: The same exchange in Matthew. Cite whichever your friend has open. The wording that matters is the same in both.
why.4Q521 (Messianic Apocalypse): A Dead Sea Scroll fragment older than Jesus. It says God's Messiah will heal, raise the dead and preach to the poor. Sealed in a cave.
why.Psalms of Solomon 17:21-32: A Jewish poem from about 50 BC praying for the 'son of David' who will reign. Shows the royal hope was specific and datable.
why.Josephus, War 6.312-313: The Jewish historian says an 'ambiguous oracle' in scripture made many expect a world ruler from Judea. A witness from the first century.

why.Jeremiah 31:31-37: Read all seven verses, not the first four. Verses 31 to 34 promise a new covenant. Verses 35 to 37 promise Israel will never cease.
why.Ezekiel 36:25-27: A parallel promise: clean water, a new heart, God's spirit within. Same idea, another prophet, also spoken to Israel.
why.Luke 22:20: 'This cup is the new testament in my blood.' The moment Christianity claims Jeremiah's promise. That is a claim, not evidence.
why.Hebrews 8:6-13: Quotes Jeremiah at length and says the first covenant is 'ready to vanish.' This is the overreach the Jewish reply rightly attacks.
why.Rashi on Jeremiah 31:30: Hebrew Bibles number this verse 31:30. Rashi reads the promise as the same Torah, finally kept. No new law, and no new people.
why.Radak on Jeremiah 31:30: Radak is David Kimhi, a commentator in Provence around 1200. He also reads renewal rather than replacement. Strong for the Jewish side.

why.Isaiah 1:18: 'Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.' The image behind the crimson thread the Talmud says stopped turning white.
why.Leviticus 16:7-10: The Day of Atonement ritual: two goats, and lots drawn between them. Read it first, or the Talmud passage will not make sense.
why.Zechariah 11:1: 'Open thy doors, O Lebanon.' The Talmud itself quotes this line about the Temple doors that opened by themselves.
why.Matthew 27:50-51: The Temple veil torn at the death of Jesus. A Christian source, and the reason the forty-year detail interests Christians at all.
why.Hebrews 9:11-12: Argues Christ entered the holy place once, with his own blood. The claim the Talmud passage is being used to support.
why.Yoma 39b: The Talmud tractate on the Day of Atonement. It records that for forty years before the Temple fell, the signs of acceptance all failed.
why.Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 6:3: The Jerusalem Talmud version of the same memory. A second Jewish record of the forty years, which is why it is worth citing.

why.Leviticus 17:11: 'It is the blood that maketh an atonement.' The verse this case turns on. Note the Jewish reply: its subject is eating blood.
why.Leviticus 16:29-34: The law fixing the Day of Atonement as a yearly statute for ever. Shows how central the altar was, which is what makes the question fair.
why.Isaiah 53:10: Calls the servant's life 'an offering for sin.' The one Tanakh text that puts a person where the sacrifice stood.
why.Hosea 3:4-5: Israel will go many days 'without a sacrifice,' then seek David their king. A Hebrew Bible text describing an age with no altar.
why.Hebrews 9:22-28: 'Without shedding of blood is no remission.' The Christian argument stated, and also where it overreaches. Read it carefully before quoting it.
why.Matthew 26:28: 'My blood of the new testament, shed for many for the remission of sins.' The claim in Jesus's own words.
why.Mishnah Yoma 8:8-9: The Mishnah is the oldest rabbinic law code, from about 200 AD. It already teaches that repentance atones. Strong for the Jewish side.
why.Avot deRabbi Natan 4: The passage where Yochanan ben Zakkai tells a student that acts of kindness now atone, quoting Hosea 6:6. The Jewish answer at its source.
why.Berakhot 26b (prayers instituted in plac: The Talmud says the daily prayers were set up to stand in for the daily sacrifices. The replacement, stated openly by the tradition.

why.Hosea 3:4-5: Many days without king or sacrifice, then a return to 'David their king.' The pattern Paul builds on, taken from the Hebrew Bible.
why.Deuteronomy 30:1-6: Scattering, then regathering, then hearts circumcised. The Torah's own promise that the story ends with Israel restored, not replaced.
why.Isaiah 29:10-14: A 'spirit of deep sleep' and a sealed book. Paul reads it as partial and passing. Isaiah was speaking first to his own generation.
why.Isaiah 59:20-21: 'The Redeemer shall come to Zion.' Paul quotes this in Romans 11:26 as his ground for saying all Israel will be saved.
why.Zechariah 12:10-13:1: The house of David mourns one pierced, then a fountain opens for sin. The same shape: grief, then cleansing, then restoration.
why.Romans 11:1-2: 'Hath God cast away his people? God forbid.' The verse that makes replacement theology a misreading of the New Testament, not a development of it.
why.Romans 11:17-29: The grafted branch, the order 'boast not,' and 'the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.' The charter Christians broke for centuries.
why.Romans 9:1-5: Paul's grief for his own people, with all their standing privileges listed. This is the tone the whole conversation should be held in.
why.Sanhedrin 97b-98a (redemption through re: Talmud pages debating whether redemption comes by repentance or on a fixed date. Worth reading: Judaism has its own version of this waiting.

why.Daniel 7:13-14: The 'son of man' who comes with clouds and is given dominion. Daniel Boyarin, a Jewish Talmud scholar, argues this figure is already divine.
why.Deuteronomy 18:15-19: God promises a prophet like Moses. Matthew's five-part structure is built on it. Jewish readers have long taken it of a line of prophets.
why.Matthew 5:17-20: 'I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil.' Read this first if the charge is that Jesus set out to abolish Torah.
why.Acts 21:20: 'Many thousands of Jews... all zealous of the law.' The earliest church, described by its own book as Torah-keeping.
why.Acts 23:6: Paul says 'I am a Pharisee' in the present tense, decades after his conversion. He never describes himself as having left Judaism.
why.Mishnah Gittin 9:10 (the Hillel/Shammai: The Mishnah records Hillel and Shammai arguing over grounds for divorce. Jesus is answering that live Jewish debate, not attacking Judaism.
why.Shabbat 31a: The Talmud story where Hillel sums up the Torah as 'what is hateful to you, do not do to others.' The same move Jesus makes.

why.Exodus 20:16: 'Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.' This covers citations. A fake Talmud quote breaks a commandment, not just an argument.
why.Proverbs 19:5: 'A false witness shall not be unpunished.' Blunt, and worth sitting with before you forward anything you have not read in full.
why.Ephesians 4:25: 'Speak every man truth with his neighbour.' The rule a Christian passing on unchecked quotations has already broken.
why.Peter Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud (on t: A Princeton scholar's calm book on the few Talmud passages that may mention Jesus. Where to go if this genuinely matters to you.
why.Sanhedrin 43a (censored text, contested: The most quoted of those passages. It was censored under Christian pressure, its dates are a century off, and scholars dispute who it means.

why.Isaiah 53:10: 'It pleased the LORD to bruise him.' On the Christian account the cross was God's own doing, which leaves no room for a blood charge.
why.Ezekiel 18:20: 'The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.' Inherited guilt is ruled out by the Hebrew Bible itself.
why.Acts 4:27-28: Names Herod, Pilate, the gentiles and Israel together. All of them did what God's hand had 'determined before.' The blame is shared, and Rome is in it.
why.Acts 3:17: Peter tells a Jerusalem crowd 'ye did it in ignorance, as did also your rulers.' The apostle closest to the events refuses the charge.
why.John 10:17-18: 'No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.' Jesus denies in advance that anyone took his life.
why.Luke 23:34: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.' Spoken from the cross. Whatever else it settles, it rules out revenge.
why.Nostra Aetate 4 (church document repudia: Not a rabbinic text. It is the 1965 Catholic declaration saying the passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews' then or now.

why.Exodus 34:6-7: God describes himself as 'merciful and gracious, longsuffering.' These verses are recited on the High Holy Days. Mercy is the centre, not an add-on.
why.Micah 7:18-19: 'Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity?' Read at the New Year. The prayer book is full of lines like this one.
why.Deuteronomy 7:7-8: God says he chose Israel not for its size or merit, but because he loved them. Election comes before obligation, in the Torah itself.
why.Romans 9:31-10:4 (Paul's actual, narrowe: Paul's actual argument is about Israel and the Messiah. He never says Jews lacked grace. The caricature misreads him as well.
why.Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1: 'All Israel has a share in the world to come.' The rabbis' own starting point is that you are in already. That is not works-righteousness.
why.Avinu Malkeinu (liturgy): The High Holy Day prayer that pleads 'be gracious to us, for we have no deeds.' Read it once and the caricature dies.

why.Deuteronomy 29:29: 'The secret things belong unto the LORD; but those which are revealed belong unto us.' The Torah's own line against hunting hidden messages.
why.Isaiah 8:19-20: Sends people to 'the law and to the testimony' rather than to those who 'peep and mutter.' The test is the plain public text.
why.Luke 24:27 (Jesus argues from the plain: Jesus explains himself from Moses and the prophets on the Emmaus road. No codes. This is the model the section follows.
why.Acts 17:2-3 ('reasoned from the scriptur: Paul argues in the synagogue by reasoning from open texts. What the earliest Christian case actually looked like.
why.Witztum-Rips-Rosenberg, Statistical Scie: The 1994 paper that started the Bible-code craze. The same journal published its refutation in 1999. Cite both or neither.
